title: All this is the Lord's
hookLine: a sage empties out everything he learned, and the sun gives him a page that starts with everything
carry: the lord lives in all this

lines: A SAGE AND AN ANGRY TEACHER.
cards: Here's how tradition says this week's text arrived. The sage Yajnavalkya, whom you met on day ten, was once the student of a great teacher, Vaishampayana.
They quarreled, and the teacher, furious, demanded back everything he'd taught him. So, in the Vishnu Purana's telling, Yajnavalkya threw it up: the whole Yajurveda, right there on the ground.
The other students turned into partridges and pecked it up. Then Yajnavalkya, emptied out, prayed to the sun. And the sun came to him as a horse and taught him verses his teacher never knew.

teach.b: Those verses became the White Yajurveda, and its closing chapter is the Isha Upanishad: eighteen verses, one page. Upanishad is usually explained as sitting down near, a student close to a teacher.
This one is named for its first word, isha, the Lord. And here's the first line: isha vasyam idam sarvam. All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is vasyam by the Lord.
Some read that word as dwelt in: the Lord lives inside everything, the way salt lives in seawater. The great teacher Shankara read it as clothed: wrap everything you see in the thought of the Lord.
Either way, this is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, said plainly. God isn't only in the temple, or up in the sky. God is in all this.
It's why many Hindus touch river water to their heads before stepping in, touch a book to the forehead if a foot brushes it, and fold their hands to a stranger.

teach.h: ALL THIS IS PERVADED BY THE LORD.
teach.b: Mahatma Gandhi is often quoted as saying that if every other scripture were lost and only this first verse remained, Hinduism would live on. So where does it meet an ordinary morning?
Many Hindus start the day looking at their open palms with a short verse. In the best-known version: Lakshmi lives at the fingertips, Saraswati in the middle, Govinda, Krishna, at the base.
Before you've touched your phone, you've seen the sacred in your own two hands.

how: Many Hindus know the Isha Upanishad's first verse by heart, and many begin the day looking at their palms with a short verse (karadarshanam) that places Lakshmi, Saraswati and Govinda in their own hands.

o: a long walk to a river for a holy bath
a sacred fire lit at the start of a rite
the Lord, the one who rules over all

games.q: what's inside today's words — tap the pairs.
p: the Lord, the one who rules
the sage the sun taught as a horse

s: in the story, the sun taught Yajnavalkya new verses
it came to him as a horse; those verses end with the Isha.
the Isha says the Lord is found only in temples
all this, whatever moves in this moving world, is the Lord's.
everyone reads vasyam the same way
some read dwelt in, pervaded; Shankara read covered, clothed.

games.q: nani touches the river water to her head before she steps in. what teaching is she living?
o: it's for luck before a swim.
the Lord lives in all this, the river too, so she greets it.
the water is cold, so she tests it first.
games.why: isha vasyam idam sarvam: all this is pervaded by the Lord. the bow is the verse, done with the hands.

practice: Open your hands in front of you and look at them, the way many Hindus do on waking. If you pray, say the line softly: isha vasyam idam sarvam, all this is the Lord's.

Then let your eyes move to whatever is near, a cup, a window, a photo of someone you love, and try the verse on each one. If you don't pray, just look, and let each thing be a little more than ordinary.

wordCard.voice: Isha, the Lord, the one who rules. Today, the first half of the Isha's first verse: all this, whatever moves, is pervaded by the Lord. Tomorrow, the renouncing and the enjoying.

orig.note: Sanskrit: isha, the Lord, the one who rules; the first word of the Upanishad and its name.

carryVoice: Your line: the lord lives in all this. Even in your own two hands. Day two hundred thirty-two.

sources.ref: Shankara, commentary on Isha Upanishad 1 (vasyam as covered)
Vishnu Purana 3.5 (Yajnavalkya gives back the Yajurveda; the partridges; the sun as a horse)
Bhagavata Purana 12.6 (the same account of the White Yajurveda)
Karadarshanam morning verse (karagre vasate lakshmih), traditional
